title: The private die report
hook: Can a distribution reveal excess high reports without identifying a liar?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish aggregate reporting evidence from accusations about individual participants.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish aggregate reporting evidence from accusations about individual participants.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: Six toy private-die reports are all six. What is their mean reported value? Toy inputs A=[6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6]; B=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[6, 3.5, 2.5], [3.5, 3.5, 0]]. Labels: Reported mean, Fair expectation, Excess mean.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The report mean differs from a fair die’s expectation, but an aggregate statistic does not reveal a particular hidden roll. The comparison shows a balanced set of reports. Stronger accusations require stronger information than these totals.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Report 1=1, Report 2=2, Report 3=3, Report 4=4, Report 5=5, Report 6=6. What is Reported mean? Answer: 3.5.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Report 1=1, Report 2=2, Report 3=3, Report 4=4, Report 5=5, Report 6=6. What is Reported mean?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 3.5. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: When people privately rolled a die and reported the result for pay, about 20% lied to the maximum and 39% were fully honest (Fischbacher & Föllmi-Heusi, 2013).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish aggregate reporting evidence from accusations about individual participants.
